parentTitle: The Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer Care
title: Delirium: prevention, 4AT and management
blurb: Spot people at risk, prevent delirium with a tailored bundle, score the 4AT correctly and manage delirium safely.
question: Mr Abbott, 86, lived independently until last week. Today on the ward he is very drowsy, keeps falling asleep mid-sentence and cannot attempt the orientation questions or the months backwards. What is his 4AT score and what does it suggest?

teach.body: Delirium is an acute confusional state: a recent change (over hours or days) or fluctuation in attention, cognition, perception, physical function or social behaviour, caused by an underlying illness, medicine or other physical stress. NICE CG103 warns it can have serious consequences, including a higher risk of dementia and death, longer hospital stays and new admission to long-term care. Plain English: the brain is telling you the body is unwell. It is common, often preventable, usually temporary, and a medical emergency until the cause is found.

teach.h: Who is at risk (assess on presentation)
head: Risk factor
Note
rows: Any one factor puts the person at risk
Past or present; confirm with a validated measure
Deteriorating or at risk of deterioration
teach.caption: CG103 rec 1.2.1. Observe at every opportunity for changes in these risk factors (1.2.2).
CG103 rec 1.3.2: be particularly vigilant for hypoactive delirium. Observe everyone at least daily for recent changes (1.5.1).

head: Item
Scores
teach.caption: 4AT user guide. Item 4 looks for change over the last 2 weeks still evident in the last 24 hours. Total 0–12.

bands.label: No delirium, no moderate-severe cognitive impairment
Suggests delirium: assess and find the cause

teach.caption: NICE CG103 rec 1.6.1: use the 4AT; in critical care or the recovery room after surgery use CAM-ICU or ICDSC instead.

teach.text: A drowsy patient who cannot answer is not 'unable to assess'. On the 4AT each untestable cognitive item scores 2, so untestable AMT4 plus untestable attention already gives 4: possible delirium. And don't use the 4AT in critical care or the recovery room: NICE says CAM-ICU or ICDSC there.

teach.h: The prevention bundle (start within 24 hours of admission)
items: Familiar staff; avoid moving the person between wards or rooms unless absolutely necessary.
Orientation: lighting, signage, a visible clock and calendar, explanations, visits from family.
Hydration and bowels: encourage drinking; manage constipation.
Hypoxia, infection (avoid unnecessary catheters) and pain, including non-verbal signs.
Mobilise soon after surgery; walking aids within reach; range-of-motion exercises.
Medication review; nutrition, with dentures that fit.
Hearing aids and glasses working and used; clear impacted ear wax.
Sleep: no procedures or medicine rounds during sleep, minimal noise.

steps.label: Find the cause
steps.sub: Identify and treat the underlying cause or causes

steps.label: Communicate
steps.sub: Reorientate, reassure, involve family and carers

steps.label: Haloperidol?
steps.sub: Short-term (usually 1 week or less), lowest dose

teach.caption: CG103 recs 1.7.1–1.7.5. Haloperidol: caution in Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies (MHRA advice).

teach.h: Scenario: Mr Abbott on the medical ward
teach.body: Mr Abbott, 86, lived independently until last week and was admitted with a urine infection. Today he is very drowsy and cannot attempt the AMT4 or months backwards. The nurse scores alertness 4, AMT4 2 (untestable), attention 2 (untestable) and acute change 4, because the clinical course clearly shows a recent change: total 12, suggesting delirium. She escalates for medical review of the cause, documents the change, keeps his glasses and hearing aids on, and talks to his daughter about what to expect.

items.label: to assess contributing factors after admission

items: Risk factors: 65+, cognitive impairment or dementia, current hip fracture, severe illness.
Observe at least daily for recent changes; hypoactive delirium is often missed.
4AT: 4 or more suggests delirium, 1–3 cognitive impairment; untestable cognitive items score 2.
Prevent with a tailored bundle within 24 hours of admission.
Treat the cause; de-escalate first; haloperidol short term, lowest dose, cautious in Parkinson's or Lewy body dementia.

summary: You can now identify people at risk of delirium, deliver the NICE prevention bundle and score the 4AT accurately. You can also manage delirium by treating the cause, de-escalating distress and using haloperidol only as NICE describes.

A.q: Four people are admitted to an orthopaedic ward. Under NICE CG103, which person is at risk of delirium because of a listed risk factor?
options: Ms Jo, 60, with well-controlled asthma
Mr Bo, 58, admitted for a hernia repair
Mr Ali, 52, with a current hip fracture
Ms Ivy, 45, with a history of migraine
A.why: CG103 rec 1.2.1 lists age 65 or over, cognitive impairment or dementia, current hip fracture and severe illness. A current hip fracture puts Mr Ali at risk despite his age.

whyNot.0: Well-controlled asthma is not a listed risk factor, and she is under 65.
whyNot.1: An elective hernia repair at 58 is not one of the four risk factors.
whyNot.3: Migraine is not a listed risk factor, and she is under 65.

A.q: Mrs Lowe, 81, is fully alert. She gets her age, date of birth and the hospital right but gives the wrong year. She says 9 months backwards correctly. Her daughter reports she has been muddled since 3 days ago. What is her 4AT score and what does it suggest?
options: 4, suggesting delirium
1, suggesting cognitive impairment
5, suggesting delirium
5, suggesting cognitive impairment
A.why: Alertness 0, AMT4 one mistake 1, attention 7+ correct 0, acute change 4: total 5. A score of 4 or more suggests delirium.

whyNot.0: The single AMT4 mistake adds 1 point, so the total is 5, not 4.
whyNot.1: This ignores the acute change item, which scores 4 when there is a recent change.
whyNot.3: The total is 5, but 4 or more suggests delirium, not cognitive impairment.

A.q: Mr Grant, 70, is in the recovery room after surgery and seems confused. Which assessment does NICE CG103 recommend in this setting?
options: CAM-ICU or ICDSC
The 4AT
The AMT4 by itself
The PRISMA-7
A.why: CG103 rec 1.6.1: in critical care or in the recovery room after surgery, use CAM-ICU or ICDSC instead of the 4AT.

whyNot.1: The 4AT is for most settings, but NICE names CAM-ICU or ICDSC for recovery and critical care.
whyNot.2: The AMT4 is one item within the 4AT and is not a delirium assessment on its own.

B.q: Which change in an 84-year-old inpatient most suggests hypoactive delirium?
options: Restless and pulling at her cannula since last night
Forgetful for 2 years, with a steady and gradual decline in memory
Withdrawn, slow to respond and eating less since yesterday
Low mood and poor sleep for the past 3 months
B.why: CG103 rec 1.3.2: hypoactive delirium shows as withdrawal, slow responses, reduced movement, poor concentration and reduced appetite, and it is a recent change.

whyNot.0: Restlessness and pulling at lines describe hyperactive delirium.
whyNot.1: A gradual decline over years suggests dementia, not an acute change.
whyNot.3: Three months of low mood fits depression rather than an acute change over hours or days.

B.q: Mr Abbott, 88, is at risk of delirium. At 22:00 the bed manager asks to move him to another ward to free a side room. What does NICE CG103 advise?
options: Move him at night when fewer people are disturbed
Move him with a family member present to settle him
Avoid moving him unless it is absolutely necessary
Move him and offer a sedative to help him settle
B.why: CG103 rec 1.4.1: care for people at risk with a familiar team and avoid moving them within or between wards or rooms unless absolutely necessary.

whyNot.0: A night move disrupts sleep, which the bundle protects, and moves are to be avoided.
whyNot.1: Family support helps, but it does not change the advice to avoid moving him.
whyNot.3: Sedation is not a prevention measure and a move should be avoided in the first place.

B.q: Mrs Ford, 83, has delirium. She is frightened and hitting out, and verbal and non-verbal de-escalation have not worked. The doctor prescribes haloperidol. Which approach matches NICE CG103?
options: Regular doses for 6 weeks, then a review
Lowest appropriate dose, usually for 1 week or less
A full dose first, reduced once she is calm
Continued at the same dose until discharge, then stopped
B.why: CG103 rec 1.7.4: consider short-term haloperidol, usually for 1 week or less, starting at the lowest clinically appropriate dose and titrating cautiously.

whyNot.0: The 6-week review applies to antipsychotics in dementia (NG97), not short-term delirium treatment.
whyNot.2: NICE says start at the lowest appropriate dose and titrate cautiously.
whyNot.3: Treatment is short term, usually 1 week or less, not linked to discharge.

C.q: Mr Abbott, 86, lived independently until last week. Today he is very drowsy, keeps falling asleep mid-sentence and cannot attempt the AMT4 or the months backwards. No relative is available. What is his 4AT score?
options: It cannot be scored
C.why: Alertness clearly abnormal 4; AMT4 untestable 2; attention untestable 2; acute change 4, because the clinical course (independent last week, drowsy now) clearly shows an acute change even without an informant. Total 12.

whyNot.1: This leaves out the acute change item, which scores 4 when the clinical course shows a clear change.
whyNot.2: This counts only the two untestable items and misses alertness and acute change.
whyNot.3: The 4AT always gives a score: untestable items score 2.

C.q: Mr Patel, 84, is admitted confused. There are no previous records, his family cannot be reached and the team cannot tell whether he has delirium, dementia or both. What does NICE CG103 advise?
options: Record dementia and refer to the memory clinic
Wait for his family before acting on the confusion
Treat it as dementia until a 4AT is repeated
Manage the delirium first
C.why: CG103 rec 1.6.3: if it is difficult to distinguish between delirium, dementia or delirium superimposed on dementia, manage the delirium first.

whyNot.0: Labelling dementia risks missing a treatable cause; NICE says manage delirium first.
whyNot.1: Waiting delays treatment of a possible medical emergency.
whyNot.2: NICE advises managing delirium first, not dementia.

C.q: Mrs Kaur, 79, is diagnosed with delirium caused by a chest infection. Where does NICE CG103 say the diagnosis should be documented?
options: In her notes and in her primary care health record
In the nursing notes for this admission
On her medicine chart beside any sedatives
In the discharge letter, if it is still present at discharge
C.why: CG103 rec 1.6.4: document the diagnosis of delirium both in the person's record or notes and in their primary care health record, because it raises future risk.

whyNot.1: Hospital notes alone miss the primary care record NICE also asks for.
whyNot.2: The medicine chart is not the place NICE specifies for the diagnosis.
whyNot.3: It should be recorded in the primary care record even if delirium has resolved.

reteach.title: Delirium is the brain's alarm
reteach.question: If you remember one thing about delirium, what should it be?

blocks.h: Something has changed, so look for why
blocks.body: Delirium is new. Dementia is gradual. When someone becomes more confused, sleepier or more agitated over hours or days, treat it as a sign of an underlying problem: infection, dehydration, hypoxia, pain, constipation, retention, medicines. Score the 4AT, escalate, and look for the cause while you keep the person safe and orientated.

blocks.text: Quiet does not mean well. A withdrawn, sleepy older person who has stopped eating may have hypoactive delirium.

explain.body: Assess risk on presentation: 65 or older, cognitive impairment or dementia, current hip fracture, severe illness. Then observe everyone in hospital or long-term care at least daily for recent changes in cognition, perception, physical function or social behaviour, and document them.

test.q: How often does NICE CG103 say people in hospital should be observed for recent changes that may indicate delirium?
options: At least weekly
At least daily
On admission
At each handover
test.why: CG103 rec 1.5.1: observe, at least daily, all people in hospital or long-term care for recent changes or fluctuations indicating delirium.

whyNot.0: Weekly is too infrequent; delirium develops over hours or days.
whyNot.2: Admission assessment is needed, but observation continues at least daily.
whyNot.3: Handover is not the NICE frequency; it is at least daily.

explain.body: Four items: alertness (0 or 4), AMT4 (0, 1, 2), months backwards (0, 1, 2) and acute change or fluctuation (0 or 4). Untestable cognitive items score 2. Total 4 or more suggests delirium; 1 to 3 suggests cognitive impairment without delirium; 0 suggests neither.

test.q: Mr Wood, 78, scores 2 on the 4AT. He is alert and there is no acute change. What does this score suggest?
options: Delirium is likely and needs urgent review
No delirium and no cognitive impairment
Possible cognitive impairment, not delirium
The test is invalid and must be repeated tomorrow
test.why: On the 4AT, a score of 1 to 3 suggests cognitive impairment but not delirium.

whyNot.0: Delirium is suggested at 4 or more.
whyNot.1: A score of 0 suggests no delirium and no moderate-severe cognitive impairment; he scored 2.
whyNot.3: A score of 2 is a valid result with its own meaning.

explain.body: Within 24 hours of admission, assess people at risk for contributing clinical factors, then deliver a tailored multicomponent package: orientation, hydration and bowels, oxygen, infection, mobility, pain, medicines, nutrition, sensory aids and sleep.

test.q: When does NICE CG103 say people at risk of delirium should be assessed for contributing clinical factors?
options: Within 72 hours of admission
Within 24 hours of admission
Once delirium is suspected
Before discharge planning starts
test.why: CG103 rec 1.4.2: within 24 hours of admission, assess people at risk for clinical factors contributing to delirium, then provide a tailored multicomponent intervention.

whyNot.3: Waiting until discharge planning misses the prevention window.

explain.body: Identify and manage the cause. Communicate, reorientate and reassure, involving family. If distressed or a risk, de-escalate first; if that fails, consider short-term haloperidol (usually 1 week or less) at the lowest dose, with caution in Parkinson's disease or Lewy body dementia. If delirium does not resolve, re-evaluate causes and assess for dementia.

test.q: Mr Diaz, 80, has delirium and is shouting and trying to climb out of bed. What does NICE CG103 advise as the first response?
options: Ask for a dose of haloperidol
Use bed rails to keep him safely in his bed overnight
Ask for a dose of lorazepam
Use verbal and non-verbal de-escalation
test.why: CG103 rec 1.7.3: if a person with delirium is distressed or a risk, first use verbal and non-verbal de-escalation techniques.

whyNot.0: Haloperidol is considered only after de-escalation is ineffective or inappropriate.
whyNot.1: Restraint is not the NICE first step; de-escalation is.
whyNot.2: Benzodiazepines are not the CG103 first response; de-escalation comes first.
